speechtext: On the Orders of the Day being called:

On a question of privilege, I wish to read this editorial which appeared in the Quebec Morning Chronicle of the 11th of March, in relation to the Battlefields Commission": Battlefields Commission.
It is interesting to note the consideration that is given by Sir George Garneau, chairman of this commission, to the many friends and adherents of his party for services in the Battlefleds Commission and the Auditor General's Report for 1912-1913, which has ju.-.t been issued gives some Interesting figures in this respect.
Sir George, evidently with great discernment and appreciations of having proper legal ser-
[Mr. Rogers. 1
vices, has looked after Mr. Antoine Galipeault, the Liberal member for Bellechasse. whose name appears in the list for legal services amounting to $5,542.27.
Mr. Lachance, the Liberal member for Quebec Centre, is also here for an item of $550, also for legal advice.
It would, of course, have been wrong to leave out the firm of Messrs. Taschereau, Rov. Cannon and Parent, but theirs is a comparatively small bill, and only amounts to $850.
Senator Choquette, however, again with his partner Mr. Galipeault, also figures for legal advice to the extent of $781.60.
Mr. L. D. Morin, another advocate here, has an item in of $500.
These several items for legal matters are extremely interesting and seem to indicate the reason why so much consideration is entertained in certain quarters for Sir George Garneau, the chairman of the commission, and why his many Liberal friends desire to keep him in such a position as to warrant the distribution of so many favours among the eminent legal fraternity of this city.
Besides the above legal expenditures, many other items are contained in the Auditor General's Report of payments made to business houses whose antipathy to the Government is well known and the attention received by them from Sir George Garneau must be very gratifying to the Liberal party as well as to themselves.
There is another article referring to the same subject in the same newspaper in its issue of the 17th of March, and before making my personal explanation, I wish to put that also upon record.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
should, as far as possible, confine his remarks to that portion of the newspaper article which refers to himself, because that is the only way in which he can raise a question of privilege.

I shall give a plain
statement of all the circumstances under which these sums of money were paid, not to me, but to the firm to which I belong, and I cannot put the full premises of my statement before the House unless I read the article. It is as follows:
Sir George Garneau explains payments-Considers the Chronicle's selection to have been an unfortunate one.
Quebec, March 16, 1914. To the Editor of The Quebec Chronicle;
Sir:-The Chronicle's leading editorial of the 12th March, attacks the chairman of the National Battlefields Commission, this time for alleged political partisanship, and to make out its case it selects from the last report of the Auditor General certain items paid to members of the Bar for legal services. The selection is an unfortunate one, however, as with one single exception, the item of $781.60, wrongly attributed to Senator Choquette, all the amounts mentioned were paid by the commission in accordance with judgments in expropriation cases, rendered by the Exchequer Court, for costs allowed by the court to the lawyers representing the Crown and the several respon-

dents, and the National Battlefields Commission had no discretion in the matter.
Under the statute 9-10 Edward VII., ch. 41, when it becomes necessary for the commission to resort to expropriation proceedings to acquire lands, these proceedings are taken, not by the commission and in its own name, but by the Attorney General for Canada (the Minister of Justice), in the name of the King before the Exchequer Court. The items mentioned in The Chronicle's article are the outcome of proceedings in expropriation initiated in June, 1910, and on which judgments were rendered by Mr. Justice Audette in May, 1912. Mr. Galipeault was appointed to represent the Crown by the then Minister of Justice, Sir Allen A,ylesworth, and the parties against whom we were proceeding were represented by lawyers, who, for obvious reasons, were not selected by the commission. These were Messrs. Rivard and Marchand, of the legal firm of Casgrain. Lavery, Rivard, Chauveau and Marchand (who figure in the Auditor General's Report for $750, but -who were overlooked by The Chronicle) ; Mr. M. J. Ahern, of Lachance and Ahern; Mr. L. D. Morin, Mr. Ferd. Roy, of Tasohereau, Roy, Cannon, Parent ; and Fitzpatrick.
Mr. Galipeault's letter, which you publish in this morning's issue of your paper, deserves careful perusal; it gives interesting facts concerning the number of cases, sixteen in all, and as in some of these cases estates comprising a large number of heirs (The Tourangeau estate and the Fages estate) were concerned, the proceedings were both complicated and costiy. I may add that the amounts involved totalled about $150,000.
Might I point out en passant that The Chronicle's article states that the different items mentioned were for 'legal advice.' The words used in the Auditor General's Report are legal expenses,' and as the two expressions are by no means equivalent the substitution of one for the other might mislead the public, a thing which I am sure The Chronicle would not like to do.
I now come to the item of $781.60, wrongly attributed to Senator Choquette. This commission is fully responsible for it. It was paid for divers disbursements and fees to the commission's legal adviser, Mr. Antoine Galipeault, who was appointed by the commission in 1908,. and it covers a period of about two and a half years. I have no doubt that you will find items under the same name in further reports of the Auditor General, as the affairs of the commission often call for the services of its solicitor.
This is the part which I wished to read to the House. This letter is from the Chairman of the National Battlefields Commission, Sir George Garneau. It explains the whole ca-se.	I have to
say that I never received a cent for legal services rendered to the Battlefields Commission or for any other kind of services. The Battlefields Commission took many actions for expropriation. Among the respondents were five or six of our clients. We took their cases in hand, brought them before the Exchequer Court, and won them; and then the court, as is
usual in such cases, condemned the Battlefields Commission, or ' the King/ as the expression is, to pay the costs. So we did not render any (legal services to the commission, our services were rendered to our clients against the Battlefields Commission.

Sword presented to Carson.
The Hon. Frank Cochrane was among a hundred hosts who paid a remarkable personal tribute to Sir Edward Carson as the Ulster leader at a demonstration dinner at the Ritz hotel last night. Other hosts were the Dukes of Rutland, Somerset, and Marlborough, Lords Milner and Selborne, and a .large company of Unionist peers and M.P.'s. also Max Aitken, Grant Morden, Donald Armour and Donald Mac-master.
There were no speeches and but three toasts, namely, 'The King,' 'Sir Edward Carson,' and 'No Home Rule.'
Surprise of the evening was the presentation to Sir Edward Carson of an infantry fighting sword with a silver scabbard and a basket hilt, and a beautifully illuminated book emblazoned with the arms of Ulster and a red hand. On the title page were the words:- 'Presented to Sir Edward by friends in Ulster in the sure confidence that God will defend the right.'
I wish only to inquire if the Prime Minister feels that it is proper for a minister of the Crown of Canada to take part in a political demonstration over as delicate a political situation as that existing in the motherland at the present time?

speechtext: On motion of Hon. J. D. HAZEN (Minister of Marine and Fisheries) the House went into Committee on Bill No. 21, to amend the law relating to merchant shipping with a view to enabling certain conventions to be carried into effect. Mr. Blondin in the Chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The Committee will remember that I introduced this Bill on the 13th of February and gave a lengthy explanation in regard to it and the matter dealt with. In the discussion which took place, the hon. member for Guysboro (Air. Sinclair), while approving of the Bill, called my attention to a point which he thought should be remedied. In consequence of this, progress was reported, although the Bill was practically agreed to, so that I might look into the point raised by the hon. gentleman. I did so, consulting with the parliamentary counsel in regard to the matter, and concluded that the point taken by the hon. member was well taken, and. that this Bill could not, for certain provisions of it, apply to the Great 
Lakes. I will propose amendments, therefore, to sections 5 and 10, which, I believe, will cover the point to which I have referred. I explained on the first reading that the Bill was the outcome of a conference in Brussels in 1910 dealing with questions of salvage	and collisions.
This convention was	signed on behalf of His Majesty, and the Maritime Conventions Act of 1911 was enacted by the Parliament of the United Kingdom to give effect to the convention. I read to the House an Order in Council passed on the report of the then Minister of Justice, Sir Allen Aylesworth, undertaking that legislation should be passed by this Parliament to give effect to that convention.
On section 2-collisions; liability for loss.

That seems to me to
make a very important change in the law.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Yes. Under the law at
present it is impossible to apportion in the way herein proposed the amount of damage where both vessels are at fault. But under this law the court will have the right to say that so much shall be borne by one vessel and so much by the other according to the degree of fault that may be found in them. This is adopted in Great Britain and the United States, and is being adopted by the other parties to the convention.
Does thiis apply to vessels of the same nation only or to vessels of different nations?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: To all vessels.

I understand that it
does not alter at all any liabilities that either vessel might have to the owner of merchandise 'that had been shipped on that vessel.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
It does not alter it at all Section agreed to.
On section 3 -loss of life and personal injuries.

This means that in cases of
accident the owners of a coasting vessel will be liable for damages to members of the crew?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 5-presumption of negligence:

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I move that subsection 1
of this section be amended by adding thereto the following words:
Except in so far as it applies to the waters described in section 10 of this Act.
Section 10 says:
This Act shall not apply to lakes Ontario, Erie, Huron (including Georgian bay), or Superior or to the river St. Lawrence above the harbour of Montreal or to vessels or rafts while navigating such waters.
We thus make the matter perfectly clear by stating just what waters are referred to.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 6-jurisdiction:
This is a new departure.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: This provides for the bringing of proceedings either in rent against the vessel, or against the owners.
The principle of taking action in rem for damages for loss of life strikes me as being entirely new.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I do not think so.
We are giving effect to what was agreed upon at the convention at Brussels by the different ship-owning nations of the world, and to what, as I have said, by Order in Council passed on the report of Sir Allen Aylesworth, this country agreed to give effect to by legislative action. The effect of this legislation is that a person who has sustained injury can bring action in one of two ways: he can bring it against the vessel, or he can bring it against the owners of the vessel, whichever he considers to be most in his interest. Most of these vessels are owned by joint stock companies with limited liabilities, .and the individual who is injured would naturally think: if I sue the company, with tneir limited liability, am I more likely to recover than if I arrest the vessel and take my action in rem aganst it.
I have no objection to the remedy at all, but I would point but that this is a new departure in this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Action in rem is not a
new departure at all so far as vessels are concerned. My hon. friend knows that in
the Admiralty court many actions in rem are taken against vessels. The vessel is arrested and bail given before it is allowed to clear.	.

Of course, that is elementary, but action in rem is confined, I think, to a very few classes of cases-for repairs, for goods supplied, for salvage, towage, and things of that sort. This legislation is creating for the first time, so far as I know, the right of sailors to bring action of this kind. I am not finding fault with it, but it is desirable to treat new legislation of that character with a great deal of care.

I understand that
the jurisdiction of the Admiralty Court iu England extends to actions in rem for personal injuries received by sailors, and I understand also that such an action could not be maintained against vessels under our Exchequer Court Act.
4	p.m. Our Exchequer Court has not the jurisdiction which the Admiralty Court in England has. I quite approve of action in rem. I am doubtful as to whether this section is full and complete enough to give this jurisdiction to our Exchequer Court. I would like the minister to look into that before the Bill ' goes through.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: This Bill was prepared by the Department of Justice for the purpose of giving effect to the convention to which I have referred. In the opinion of the Department of Justice it does give effect to it, though I have never before heard discussed the point raised by the hon. member for Sunbury and Queens. But if we pass this legislation now, surely under that law the Exchequer Court would have jurisdiction to consider cases coming before it.

It would, if the machinery is 'complete enough. Another matter I would like to mention is that of damages done by Government vessels. If a Government vessel runs into another vessel owned by private persons, an action in rem cannot be sustained against the Government vessel itself?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Of course, Government vessels are in rather a different plane from vessels belonging to private owners. Vessels belonging to private ship-owners are in one part of the world one week and in another part of the world the next. Unless you were able to arrest the vessel in the port where the accident occurred, the

claimant might lose his remedy for the owners of the vessel might not be responsible people, and if a person aggrieved could not bring an action in trem, he might have to follow that vessel over half the world before he could take action and recover the damages to which he was entitled. In the case of a Government-owned vessel, the situation is different: the Government is always in existence, the King is never dead, and if an injury is done by a Government vessel there is no need of arresting it, because, if the party whose vessel has been injured has a proper claim, he can bring action against the Government by petition of right as in all other cases. I assume that is the case, although I am not aware whether there is any special provision in the law relating to this matter.

I was under the same impression until, on looking into the question, I found that there is a decision of our Exchequer Court, confirmed by the Dominion Supreme Court, to the effect that a petition of right cannot be filed in a case of that kind. I know of a case exactly in point where the collision was caused by the negligence of a Government vessel. It was held by the. court that a petition of right could not be sustained.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Then what remedy have
you? Is there any remedy?
That is what I want to ask the minister-if he will provide a remedy in such a case.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: In case of a collision between a Government-owned and a private-owned vessel, if the Government vessel is in default, is there no remedy which the private-owned vessel can have other than by the grace of the Crown? Is there no process by which the private-owned vessel can bring an action in any court against the Government because of that damage?

The only remedy now is to bring a personal action against the captain with the hope that the Government will pay any verdict that might be recovered against him. That 5s one of the difficulties in our law at present, that in Canada a petition of right would not lie in such a case. I understand that vessels chartered and under Government control stand in the .same position as Government-owned vessels. The point I want to make is that, in such a case as I have mentioned, there should be some remedy or means by which such claims could be investigated 
and decided, eitner by the Admiralty Court or the Exchequer Court, or by some official acting as an arbitrator.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The question raised by my hon. friend is one that certainly is well worthy of consideration. I was always under the impression that in a case of that sort the owner of the vessel aggrieved could file a petition of right and have the matter tried out in the Exchequer Court, as in the case of any other claim against the Government. My hon. friend, who has had wide experience and is in a position to speak with authority, says that is not the case. I will give the matter consideration and discuss it with some of the law officers of the Crown in Ottawa, and ascertain the exact position, because it seems to me that there ought to be some Temedy for the private vessel owners. I do not think that any government would want any private owner to suffer through the wrong or default of its property or its officers. It is not however, a matter, that properly comes within the purview of this Bill. This is merely to give effect to the convention, and perhaps it would be impossible to take the matter up seriously with a view to having action at this session, but I will certainly give consideration to it to see what remedy ought to be applied.

I think that under the present state of the law a vessel under contract or charter to the Government is in the same position as a private-owned vessel. I certainly would not like to see Parliament place Government-owned vessels in the same position as private-owned vessels, so that persons could bring actions in rem against them.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not see why an action in rem should be brought against a Government vessel, because you are sure of your damages if you recover. But it seems to me that there ought to be some court or procedure, by which you could have the matter tried out and a judical decision given.

According to the law as stated by the hon. member for Sunbury and Queens (Mr. H. H. McLean), it would appear that the Petition of Right Act was held by the court not to cover this point. Then the minister could very simply meet this difficulty by amending the petition of right chapter of the law so as to cover this particular point so that a petition of right, could be brought and a Temedy could be obtained in court in a ease of this kind as

well as in other cases. It would appear that under the law as it exists now this class of cases cannot be dealt with by petition of right. It says:
The amount shall he apportioned by the court or person making the apportionment in accordance with the law of the country to which the vessel belongs.
That is the crew may -be of different nationalities, but it is the law of the country in which the vessel is owned that prevails in the dividing of the salvage between the parties?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes, as to the apportionment. If a German vessel were awarded damages, say, at Quebec, these damages would be apportioned among the officers and crew of the vessel according to the law of Germany where the vessel belongs. If a Canadian vessel were awarded damages by the Admiralty Court in France, the Admiralty Court judge would award the damages according to the 'law of Canada. I think that is perfectly proper and I think anything else would not be proper because it is only right that they should get these damages according to the laws of the country where they belong.
That is a change in the law?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Yes, and I think a very
good change.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 9-time limited for bringing action for damages to two years and for contribution to one year:

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
An action for damages or salvage must be commenced within two years and an action for the recovery of contribution must be commenced within one year. It will be observed that there is power given to the court to extend this period under such conditions as it thinks fit and it shall,
-if satisfied that there had not during any such period been any reasonable opportunity , of arresting the defendant vessel within the jurisdiction of the court, or within the territorial waters of the country to which the plaintiff ship belongs or in which the plaintiff resides or has his principal place of business, extend any such period to an extent sufficient to give such reasonable opportunity.
It seems to be well that that power shomd be given to the judge in order that no injustice may be done.

It seems very reasonable, but I notice that it provides that an action for damages against a vessel must be taken
within two years while an action for recovery of contribution must be taken within one year. Is there any reason why there should be this difference?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I must confess that I do not see any very good reason for the difference, but still that is what was agreed to by the parties to the convention and I do not like to change it. But this proviso gives ample power to the judge to extend the time.

What is meant by
' rules of the court '? I do not know of any rules of the court that would cover a case of this kind. This is a new jurisdiction altogether.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Is it not a fact, that the Exchequer Court which now deals with all these Admiralty cases, has power to make rules from time to time as cases arise, and, if it is necessary to make rules to govern these cases, will it not have power to do so just as it would in other cases? I think the Exchequer Court has power now to make rules under the Exchequer Court Act. I am not sure whether they have to be approved by the Governor in Council but I think they have.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 10-Act not to apply to Great Lakes, etc.:

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I do not think this is perfectly clear as if reads at present:
This Act shall not apply to lake Ontario, Erie, Huron (including Georgian bay), or Superior or to the river St. Lawrence above the harbour of Montreal or to vessels or rafts while navigating such waters.
This convention, I may say, deals with questions of the sea and not with questions of the lakes, and it may be very desirable that in the future the same rules should apply to the lakes. But there is no use applying these rules to the lakes until similar rules are adopted by the Government of the United States. The vessels that traverse the lakes are the vessels of the United States and of Canada. Collisions may occur between those vessels and the rules of this country and their rules should be the same. The matter of applying the rules to the lakes, if the United States adopt this agreement, will have to be taken up at some future time and farther legislation will have to be asked from this House making the rules applicable to the United States, but until the United States shall agree to do the same thing it would be a purposeless, useless and unwise thing to do. I would

move to strike out subsection 1 and suo-stitute the following:
This Act shall not apply to lakes Ontario Erie, St. Clair, Huron, (including Georgian bay), Superior, or to the river St. Lawrence above the harbour of Montreal, or to the St. Mary, St. Clair or Detroit rivers, or to the Sault Ste. Marie, Welland or St. Lawrence canals, or to vessels or rafts while navigating such waters.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Amendment agreed to, and section as amended agreed to.
On the preamble:

It would be desirable
if these regulations were made a schedule to the Act-

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
This is giving legislative
enactment to tne convention. [DOT]
They must have passed a body of rules, and it would be desirable to have them mentioned in a schedule to the Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I do not think they did.
I think they made a report recommending that these, things be done, and then the different countries agreed to give legislative enactment to them.
They must be put in some shape somewhere.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
They were put in shape
by the law officers in Great Britain, and to that extent we were able to avail of their work. The convention has been put in force in the United States, and in mo-at of the other countries. The convention laid down the principles which they thought ought to govern, and it was agreed by the members of the convention that they would adhere to them, if their countries passed legislation with respect to them.
Copies of the conference dealing with collisions and salvage were transmitted to the Canadian Government for consideration in Colonial Office Despatch, dated 28th September, 1906. Following the practice of the Imperial Board of Trade in dealing with such matters in the United Kingdom, the Department of Marine and Fisheries invited the views of the Shipping Federation of Canada -and the Boards of Trade of Montreal, Quebec, Halifax, St. John, Charlottetown, Victoria and Vancouver, on the proposed conventions. Mr. F. E. Meredith,
K.C., solicitor of the Shipping Federation of Canada submitted a very valuable opinion dealing fully with the questions from a legal standpoint. The Boards of Trade of Montreal and Victoria also submitted their

views in regard to the conventions. Papers were subsequently referred to the Department of Justice for consideration, and the Hon. Mr. Aylesworth, Minister of Justice, wrote to the Hon. Mr. Brodeur, Minister of Marine and Fisheries, under date of the 23rd January, 1907, as follows:
I would suggest that in your report to Council you should set out the steps taken by you to ascertain the views of the commercial and shipping interests pf Canada, and attach copies of the replies of the Montreal Board of Trade and tlie Shipping Federation of Canada, including Mr. Meredith's report, as well as a copy of the report of the Victoria Board of Trade. I would also suggest that the Imperial authorities be informed that while Canada is willing to concur in any action for the putting into force these two conventions that Great Britain may think proper to adopt, Canada would urge in view of her very extensive inland navigation in which Canadian vessels are in constant intercourse with vessels belonging to the United States, that if the conventions are put in force their provisions should extend to the inland waters of Canada, and to vessels for inland navigation of any of the waters of Canada or the inland waters of Canada or the United States contiguous to Canada,
An Order in C-ouncil passed on the 6th May, 1907, embodying Mr. Aylesworth's suggestions, except that no -copies of replies received by the department were forwarded. It- w-as also suggested that His Majesty's Government should ascertain the views of the United States Government on the question of extending the convention to cover inland waters. But it was expressly -stated that the Canadian Government did not desire to delay -action on account of this inquiry.

This is of far-reaching importance to Canadian shipping. Under the British North America Act it would appear that we have almost unlimited power to legislate in connection with every conceivable subject that comes within the purview of this Parliament, but there always has been a defect in our power to deal with the law of shipping. It seems to always have been the rule that, in a general way, shipping legislation cannot become the law of this country until it receives the approval of the Crown through the Government of Great Britain. I have never been very clear as to why this is so. I understand that there was some provision in the old Shipping Act of 1854, which limited the jurisdiction of colonial parliaments, and it is held, I believe, that this restriction which was created in that Act, was never removed, notwithstanding the British North America

Act. It is desirable that in Canada we should have no trammels whatever with respect to any of our legislation. I call the attention of the minister to the desirability of having this disability, as far as our Parliament is concerned, removed, if it can be done without any wrench to our constitutional relations with the mother country.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I will consider the matter.
I do not quite know what is involved, but I will make careful inquiry into it and be able to give some information to my hon. friend at a subsequent period.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Preamble agreed to, and Bill reported.

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext: On motion of Hon. J. D. HAZEN (Minister of Marine and Fisheries), Bill No. 104, respecting the Harbour of North Sydney in Nova Scotia, was read the second time, and the House went into Committee thereon, Mr. Blondin in the Chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
As I explained before, this Bill is to abolish the Harbour Commission at North Sydney and is introduced at the request of the board of trade, and of a large number of individuals and, also in compliance with very largely signed petitions. The mayor of the town of North Sydney came here asking that this should be done. I explained the reasons to the House before. North Sydney harbour is situated very close to Sydney harbour. It is felt that North Sydney harbour is somewhat discriminated against by having this Harbour Commission, because a much larger sum is collected in that harbour in tolls and fees from the ships than is collected in Sydney harbour. It is felt that thi^ discriminates against the welfare of North Sydney.
I stated to the House that North Sydney, the total collections in 1912, from the tax under which there is levied on all registered vessels of foTty tons or over a due of one cent a ton, amounted to $3,792.60. Out of this amount are paid salaries to the commissioners. the harbour-master, etc. My hon. friend from North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) asked me if, when the Bill went into committee, I would have, the information showing the fees collected in Sydney. In 1911, the fees collected in Sydney on ships were $312; in 1912, $343; in 1913, $350. Out of these amounts ,the harbour-master receives the sum of $300 annually as salary. The rates charged at Sydney-and the same rates will be charged at North Sydney after
these Acts are repealed and North Sydney passes under the provisions of the Harbour
Masters' Act-are as follows:

under	$0	50
For every ship of fifty tons register and
not over 100 tons register	 1 00
For every ship of 100 tons register and
not over 200 tons register	 1 50
For every ship of 200 tons register and
not over 300 tons register	 2 00
For every ship of 300 tons register and
not over 400 tons register	 2 50
For every ship of 400 tons register and
not over 500	tons register	 3	00

This will be the ordinary rate charged in harbours where there is no commission or as to which there is no special legislation. The collections can be made only twice bn the same ship in any one year. Of course, a ship might be making regular trips to and from a port, but the collections can be made only on two trips each year. Out of these rates a salary will be paid to the harbour-master, who will collect the tolls and take charge of the harbour, performing the usual duties that harbour-masters perform.
On the first reading of this Bill I informed the House that I proposed to add this section:
This Act will come into force on the 1st day of January, 1915.
It is thought wise to do this in order that there may not be any difficulty about adjusting matters that are outstanding when the powers of the commission will expire.

Are the dues which
my hon. friend has enumerated the same as those now collected in Sydney harbour?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.

In North Sydney we
have a magnificent piece of valuable Government property called the ballast ground. There is also the right-of-way bought by the commission extending to that ground, and some other property which will have to be looked after by somebody. I suppose that the department will make some regulation by which that property will be looked after and kept in proper condition. The commission, while they were not able to do very much, were always able with what money they were collecting to keep this property in good shape. A breakwater at the end of the harbour was also kept in good condition by the commission. When the commission goes out of existence

nobody will have control over this property.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
It is provided by this
Bill that all the assets of the commission shall pass into the hands of the Government, which will become responsible for the liabilities of the commission. The liabilities at the present time are small, I think about $800. The breakwater will become a public work and will be managed by the Deparment of Public Works, which will attend to its repairs and give it the attention that may be necessary, and any public works required in the harbour will be attended to from time to time by the Department of Public Works, which will ask Parliament for appropriations for the purpose, just as in the case of many other harbours in Nova Scotia and other parts of Canada. So far as the ballast ground is concerned, I suppose that ships discharge ballast there and take ballast from there?

That is the way in
which the property was created, and it is still called the ballast ground.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: What is it used for now?

It is not used for anything, but ships lie around it and use the breakwater as a wharf. It is a large piece of property, and we are always proud of saying that it is capable of becoming one of the most magnificent termini of Canada for shipping, if we can get it into proper shape. Of course, we always felt that it was an advantage to have it, because being Government property, no person could charge anything for the use of it.
Mr. . HAZEN:	The wharfs in various
harbours are built by the Department of Public Works or under its control and management. When they are completed, they are transferred to the Department of Marine and Fisheries and are subject to dues and tolls. The Department of Marine and Fisheries initiates the step by which wharfingers are appointed to collect the tolls. As a matter of fact, many of them receive very small salaries. If that wharf is a breakwater, it will come under the control of the Department of Public Works, but if this ballast ground is used as a landing place for ships, then I presume it will come under the control of the Department of Marine and Fisheries. If repairs of an extensive character have to be made, then, according to the present practice, they would have to be done by the Department of Public Works.
[Mr. McKenzie !

Has the minister
given any attention to the question whether or not he will continue the present harbour master in his position?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I have not considered the matter at all. That question will not arise for some time.

The minister must
know that the present harbour-master is a good staunch Tory, appointed since the change of Government. While I am speaking in his interest, I am not speaking of any person who supports me. He is an exceedingly capable man, an old deep-sea captain who has travelled the world over. He has retired from seafaring life, but I do not know of a more capable man for the position of harbour-master while it is in his power to perform the work. When other days come, we will look after him.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The hon. gentleman surely would not turn him out?

I wish to bring this
information to the knowledge of the minister, so that, in case of any representations being made to him, he may know that the present holder, of the office is an exceedingly capable man and knows the business of harbour-master better than many people who might be looking for appointments.
I am quite aware of the practice of the Public Works Department in building wharfs and passing them over to the Marine and Fishefies Department. I am sorry that the Government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier passed a law under which the Marine and Fisheries Department is given power to impose fees for the use of these wharfs. I acknowledge our transgression in this regard; I was here myself and gave passive support-involuntary passive support-to that Act. But it is working great hardship and injustice to the fishermen along the coast of Victoria. I trust the minister will give up the barbarous idea of charging a fisherman because he spreads his net on the breakwater. These wharfs were built largely as shelters and breakwaters for the boats of the fishermen, and the present Administration have appointed men to look after them as wharfingers and harbour-masters. Dues are collected if a fisherman spreads his nets ox lands fish on the breakwater or does anything else necessary in his calling This is a small matter so far as the revenue collected is concerned, and I am sure the minister will not care twopence for what is collected, while the charge is an extreme hardship for the fishermen.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
There are other classes besides the fishermen affected by this matter. In many cases farmers use Government wharfs to ship their produce to market. In most oases the fees amount to a very small .sum, and we have been considering whether, in the case of farmers and fishermen, it would not be better to abolish the fees altogether. On the other hand there must be isomdbody to take care of the wharf and somebody who is responsible, and that some one must be paid for his services. The question arises whether the wharfinger shall be paid a certain sum out of the general revenues of the country, or whether, as at present, he shall be paid a percentage of the fees he collects. The hon. gentleman knows that it would not do to apply the principle he speaks of to all Government wharfs, for some are used for commercial purposes and yield a considerable revenue. For instance, the department owns a wharf in *the haTbour of St. John over which a great deal of trade passes every year, and to which vessels resort. It would be impossible to remove these fees. It would be necessary to limit it to certain classes of wharfs. For the wharfs along the rivers, such as the St. John river, it should include the farmers. The fees are sometimes more vexatious than anything else, and the total collections in some cases are so small that it is impossible to get any one in the neighbourhood to take charge of the wharf. The whole question is being considered. I have taken it up once or twice with some of my officials, and perhaps we can woTk out some plan that will be satisfactory.
Mr. H. H. MeLEAN: I am glad to hear what the minister says about the wharfs on the river St. John. As the hon. minister knows, some wharfs on that river have been built by the Dominion Government and others by the local Government. No wharfage is charged on those wharfs built by the local Government, and of course it is a hardship to farmers who have to pay fees on the wharfs built by the Dominion. I am glad to heaT the minister say that no charge will be m.ade on Government wharfs, for example, on the river St. John.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I move that the following be added as section 4:
This Act shall come into force on the 1st clay of January, 1915.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Amendment agreed to, and section as amended agreed to.
Bill reported.

speakerposition: subtopic

speakeroldname: Hon. J. D. HAZEN (Minister of Marine and Fisheries):
speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: If there is no objection, we will take up Bill No. 71, to consolidate and amend the Act respecting Fisheries and Fishing. A number of amendments were made to this Bill by the Committee on Marine and Fisheries, and the Bill as amended has been reprinted, but I understand that only a few copies have been circulated, and so, except with the approval of the hon. gentleman (Mt. GraHam), leading the other side of the House, I cannot take it up.
I think it is all right.
Does this relate only to salt water fishing?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
No, to fishing generally. I may say that this Bill was thoroughly explained by me on the 16th of February on its first reading. Later, on my motion, it was referred to the Select Standing Committee on Marine and Fisheries. That committee held altogether three meetings for the discussion of the Bill, and gave its provisions very careful attention. The committee suggested certain amendments, which amendments have been incorporated in the Bill; and, as the measure left the committee, I think there was practically no objection to it, as the members of the committee seemed to agree that the amendments we made were in the interests of the public and the fishermen. The Bill is *quite satisfactory to myself and to the officials of the department.
The House went into Committee on the Bill, Mr. Blondin in the Chair.
In some cases the powers of justices of the peace are conferred upon fishery officers. In what cases and under what circumstances is this authority given by the Government?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Every case stands on its
own merits. In some sections of the country, especially in the northern portions of Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia, there are no justices of the peace and, in order to have any enforcement of the law at all, or any tribunal before which information can be laid and matters tried, it is necessary to appoint these officers

justices of the peace. These are not the only places where such officers are appointed, although a large number of the officers are not vested with this power. I do not think we have ever had a case where a fishery officer has made an arrest and then tried the case himself as justice of the peace. Under this Act we are extending the power of appeal. Under the old Act the only appeal was to the minister; under this Bill we are giving the power to appeal to a judge of the county court. In view of those two powers of appeal, one to the county court judge and the other to the minister, and of the necessity that exists in parts of the country for conferring'this power, the committee, after fully discussing the matter, decided that the Act should be left as it is.

In my humble opinion, this practice is absolutely contrary to the method in which law should be enforced in this country. In the county of Inverness the fishery officers in the old days were given this jurisdiction, and invariably they tried the cases themselves. There was no appeal then, and perhaps it makes it a little easier for the person who does not receive justice in such cases to have recourse to a higher court. But it is a hardship on the person who does not receive justice in the court below to appeal, and I think this Act should be amended so as to cover only the cases to which my hon. friend has referred. In Nova Scotia there are very many rivers, and in those districts there are innumerable justices of the peace -too many. I think it is against the spirit of British law and British fair play that the man who lays the information or who is directly concerned in laying the information with regard to an infraction of the law should try the case himself.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The same practice exists in connection with the mounted police.

If it does, it is wrong; the principle is absolutely wrong. I care not how fair a fishery officer may be. there is the temptation on his part to render a verdict against a man in a case in which he is directly interested. I be-5 p.m. lieve that the minister would be doing justice if he would confine appointments of these ex-officio officers to places such as he points out, where it is impracticable to carry out the law in any other way. In Nova Scotia there is no necessity for any such law as this. I am not condoning the man who violates the fishery regulations, but if
[Mr. Hazen.1
we are to have the matter properly adjusted, it must be adjusted before a justice of the peace or a stipendiary magistrate who is not in any way connected with the case. This is an old grievance in our province. This is not the first time I have brought the matter to the attention of the Government of this country. I brought it to the attention of the late Government by memorial several times, and I am sorry to say that I got very little redress. I think the minister would meet with considerable approbation in our part of the country if he were to arrange this matter in some way so that fishery officers would not act in their own cases.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: This provision has been in the Act for a great many years, and since I have been in the department no complaint has been brought to me, from Nova Scotia or elsewhere, that any injustice has been done. The statement made to me by the fishery officials of my department is that this power has been sparingly exercised, and I may say that my intention is to exercise it only in those cases in which it is necessary to do so. I realize that there is a great deal of force in what my hon. friend says, but it would be impossible, in a Bill like this, to define the different districts in which these appointments should be made. They have to be made in certain parts of the country if we are to have any enforcement of the law at all. That being the case, I think it would be a pity to strike this provision out of the Act, and I will insist, as far as I can, upon its going in. All statutes are liable to some abuse. No matter how carefully the statute is drawn, there is scarcely a case in which there cannot be some abuse or some injury under the law. But in passing laws we have to act on the assumption that discretion will be exercised and that common sense will prevail. If it is found in the future that abuses arise and that the liberty of the subject is interfered with in any way, I do not hesitate to say, in view of the discussion that has taken place to-day, that 1 would consider very seriously some amendment which would cover those sections of the country where we have to have these officials. I do not think, however, that a-the* present time there are abuses which make this necessary, and I hope that my hon. friend will not urge his objection.

Did I understand the
minister to say that under the provisions of the law the same person is prosecuting officer and judge?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No, that has never occurred in a single instance. But there were certain fishery officers named by the Governor in Council who might be authorized by the Governor in Council to exercise the powers of a justice of the peace. This Act makes these officers ex officio justices of the peace within the districts for which they are appointed to act as fishery officers; but a case has never occurred where the fishery officer has laid a complaint and then has sat to try the case.
Oh, yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
If an appeal were made
to me from a decision of that sort, I would consider it an absolute outrage, and would at once reverse the decision. In the northern parts of Saskatchewan and Alberta there are districts where there are no justices of the peace. This gives these fishery officers the same powers as are given to mounted policemen in those districts.

There is a vicious principle running through this legislation, that a man charged with a certain duty as a fishery officer for the prevention of offences against the Fishery Act, who becomes by authority of his office a prosecutor, is clothed with the powers of a magistrate, so that he is permitted to act upon a case in which he is practically, no matter who lays the actual complaint, the real prosecute." and also the judge. It seems to me that two of the arguments that have been used as reasons for the continuance of this legislation are rather weak. One is its antiquity. That is a<n argument which it is not necessary to controvert, because it controverts itself. The fact that a wrong has been perpetrated for a long time .is no reason why the wrong should continue. Therefore we can set aside at once the argument of antiquity. As to those- districts which are so remote that it is impossible to get a magistrate-and I have never seen a district so remote-the appeal would be no protection at all, because the parties are so far away that the expense of an appeal would very far outweigh any resulting advantage. Except for very special occasions, this is legislation that should not be permitted. The Governor in Council might take power under this Bill to pass an Order in Council, under certain circumstances, especially appointing some officer in such a remote district as the minister speaks of, with power to act as a magistrate as well as a preventive officer; but if this applies all
over the country, as I understand it does, it is very vicious and bad legislation that should be wiped off the book.
Has the hon. member considered the question of our jurisdiction to pass legislation providing for the appointment of magistrates, which is a matter falling within the powers of the provinces?

I had not considered
that phase of the question, but of course this Government could ask to have them appointed by the provincial authorities.

Why could not the provincial Government be requested to appoint the fishery officers justices of the peace? The case of the mounted police is not on all fours. The mounted police are patrolling the whole country and they must have the right to mete out swift justice. It should not be permitted that a man could lay the information and try the case. In such a case an appeal is not sufficient.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That is not the case.
The Government may appoint ex officio justices of the peace who are fishery inspectors. Such an officer would lay the information and try the case, and then you give the right of appeal.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman is
wrong in saying he lays the information.
He prosecutes.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: He does not.
Then who sets the law in motion?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: One of these fishery officers, and he goes before a justice of tfie peace. It may be that the justice before whom he goes is another fishery officer who is invested with this power.
The minister says that it never occurs that an officer lays the information and tries the case. How does the minister know it?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
It has never occurred
since I became fiead of the department.

Perhaps it has not come to the minister's notice because there has been no appeal, as the expense of an appeal, owing to the long distance at which the person involved lives from the place where the appeal would be heard, makes it impossible for him to take the appeal, and he would prefer to suffer trie wrong

and injury. The minister cannot say it has never occurred; it is more probable that it has occurred many times than that it has never occurred, and that these men have put up with the injustice. I think the best way would be to wipe out the legislation.

I am not opposing this clause of the Bill for tfie mere purpose of opposition. I want to point out that for years Mr. A. C. Bertram, fishery officer for the island of Oape Breton, tried all his own cases, and in those days there was no appeal'to a higher court. Mr. James Cody, who was fishery officer in that section of the country before Mr. Bertram was appointed, also tried all his own cases. There was no appeal in those days to a higher court. Mr. Bertram, a gentleman for whom I had the greatest regard, and who is now dead, probably tried those cases very fairly, but a great many objections were taken at that time. Mr. Bertram lived at North Sydney. There were fishery guardians who had been recommended by him and who were appointed by the fishery [DOT]officer. When they got information tend. ing to show that a person was contravening the regulations they would lay that information before their chief, Mr. Bertram, who would try the case and collect the costs because he was a stipendiary justice of the peace. From his decision there was no appeal. That was carried on year after year. If what the minister says is correct, that no officer will try a case in his own jurisdiction, what is the necessity for this legislation at all? The jurisdiction of the fishery officer is very large. In the four [DOT]counties of Cape Breton there is only one fishery officer.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Only one inspector.
Inspector, or fishery overseer.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Guardian.

Guardians are not fishery [DOT]officers. They are simply appointed temporarily in the summer. If the fishery [DOT]officers do not try, and are not supposed to try, their own cases at the present time, why appoint them ex-officio justices of the peace?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The fishery guardian lays the information, not before himself, because he has no power, but before one of the gentlemen who is an inspector in his district. That does not mean that he is trying it himself. If a fishery inspector happened to be one of those who is vested
[Hr. Fowler. 1
with this power, can you imagine the inspector laying the information before himself and trying the case himself? It may be the overseer who is vested with this power. The officers of the department tell me that it is absolutely necessary, if we are going to try to get our fishery act enforced that this power should be vested in these officers. There is no provision of the Act that they are more opposed to having cut out than this provision. They do not believe that any injury will result to anybody as a consequence of it. I do not suppose that there is any such state of affairs existing as my hon. friend has spoken of as having existed in Mr. Bertram's day. My hon. friend has spoken in regard to the fact that the inspector is, in a way, over these other men, and would naturally be influenced by what these other guardians or overseers would say. The same thing is absolutely true in many cities and towns throughout the country where the police magistrate is responsible for the conduct of the police force. In many cases the police magistrate is a member of the police commission which appoints the policemen. Yet, it is not claimed that a police magistrate should not try an offence because the information might be laid by a policeman appointed by himself. You might as well argue that a police magistrate would be influenced by a policeman, owing to the fact that he is responsible for his appointment. The officers of the department are sincere in their belief that it is necessary that we should have this provision if we want the Act enforced. But if it is brought to my attention in the future that it has caused any hardship-which it has not done in the past for a great many years-we will try and deal with the matter in some other way. The committee of the House on Marine and Fisheries considered the whole thing and reported this provision favourably.
Now, I would like to say a word in reply to the matter brought up by my hon. friend from Richmond (Mr. Kyte). In the Act as inserted he will see this provision:
A moiety of every pecuniary penalty levied by virtue of this Act shall belong' to His Majesty, and the other moiety shall he paid to the prosecutor other than a fishery officer or fishery guardian.
This is taken* out because it was felt by the committee that the provision in the old Act under which the informer got half of the fine was not a desirable one as it was too great an incentive to the fisharv

officer to lay an information, -where perhaps he would not he justified in doing so.
If I could get from the minister the assurance that he would not give any person in Nova Scotia any such authority as this I would not oppose it any further.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There are some who have that authority now.

They should not have it. It is provided that .a person shall be exofficio a justice of the peace in the district for which he is appointed to act as fishery officer. We will take the Margaree river over which there is one fishery officer and from eight to twelve guardians. These guardians are supposed to watch at night and they may suspect a man of poaching or of illegally setting a net. They are directly responsible to the fishery officer who has jurisdiction as a justice of the peace in that vicinity. The guardian is called upon to go before the fishery officer and lay an information and the fishery officer, being a justice of the peace, is empowered to try the case. He is directly interested in securing a conviction against all poachers, and this is an instance where a person is the judge in his own case. He is interested in his capacity as a fishery officer and in many other ways. Why should there be any necessity for such a thing? In the -province of Nova Scotia, I am sorry to say, there is a justice of the peace in almost every house. It is an outrage that a fishery officer should be given such powers when we have men at every angle of the road, at every turn, some of whom are capable and some otherwise, of enforcing the law. I can see some force in the argument of the minister as regards outlying districts in the West, hut surely in the Maritime provinces there does not exist any necessity for appointing a fishery officer as a justice of the peace, a fishery officer who will he trying a case within his own jurisdiction the information in which has been laid before him by one of his -subordinate officers. I am not going to oppose the matter any further than to say I think the minister should not appoint in the Maritime provinces at least any fishery officer a justice of the peace to try these cases.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: My hon. friend may rest assured that I will not appoint them unless I think they are necessary.

I know something about Nova Scotia and the stipendiary magis-114
trates and I cannot -conceive of any part of the province where it is necessary to appoint a fishery officer a justice of the peace to carry out the regulations of the Fisheries Department. It is not according to British principles of fair play and justice and I hope it will not he done.

The criticism directed against this section, appears in the mind of my hon. friend from South Cape Breton (Mr. Carroll) to have reference to poaching along rivers. We will take, for instance, the case of a lobster factory. The fishery officer has jurisdiction to see that the regulations in regard to legal packing of -lobsters are carried out. There is no guardian who has any jurisdiction in regard -to the matter. The fishery officer comes along and v-isits the lobster factory. He finds a seed lobster on the premises of the lobster packer. Under this section the inspector has the right to lay an information, to issue a summons and to try the case. There is no other person to co-oper-ate with him in enforcing the law. This section would be useless if it were necessary to call in some other person to enforce the law with him. I knew of a case, during the incumbency of the late Mr. Bertram in the office of fishery inspector, on the island of Cape Breton.
Mr. Bertram was endeavouring to enforce the size limit, and, visiting the factory, he -saw the shell of a lobster which apparently in life -had been undersized, and he -said to the packer, 'You- have violated the law.' The lobster packer denied that such was the case, but Mt. Bertram said: 'Here is the body of this lobster which I have found on the shore adjoining the factory, and it is under size.' Mr. Bertram considered that this evidence was sufficient to justify him in convicting the lobster packer for violating the regulations. Mr. Bertram himself laid the information; he issued the ordinary process; he tried the case, and he convicted the lobster packer. I do not think for a moment that Mr. Bertram was not acting conscientiously in endeavouring to carry out the law; he knew that it was extremely difficult to detect infractions of the size limit, and he felt that in this case he would make the lobsteT packer pay the fine. But I do not think that any independent justice of the peace would ever have convicted the lobster packer upon such evidence. Under this -section, I understand, the same thing may happen. We all know that the fishery officers UTe not selected for their



qualifications to carry out the law, or to administer it, or to interpret it, but that they are selected because of other considerations. I am not going to say that every justice of the peace in Nova Scotia is absolutely competent to properly inter. pret the law, but there is, at least, a presumption that the justices of the peace are impartial, and that they will give such judgment as their knowledge of the law and the evidence will enable them to give. I objected to this section in the committee, but the majority was against me. I support the argument of the member for South Cape Breton, and ask that the operation of this section be suspended so far as Nova Scotia is concerned.

I agree thoroughly with all
that has been said by the hon. member for South Cape Breton (Mr. Carroll). In addition to the reasons he has given, there are two other reasons why this section should be omitted from the Act. Fishery inspectors are appointed purely for political reasons, and when there is a change of Government, no doubt the men appointed by the present Government will have to leave office, so that they are not in an independent position to decide as to whether a man is or is not guilty of a violation of the Fisheries Act. I do not say that because a man is a Conservative he would convict a Liberal more readily than he would a Conservative, but I do think they are, most of them anyway, prone to lean to their own political side. Another objection I have to this provision is, because of the large areas over which these inspectors have jurisdiction. Mr. Fisher, for instance, has jurisdiction over Shelburne, Queens, Yarmouth, Digby, Annapolis, and, I think, Hants, and it appears to me that there would be great expense and delay caused, if Mr. Fisher, who might be in Lunenburg, had to be sent for to try a trivial offence against the Fisheries Act in the county of Hants. It wouM be much more satisfactory all around, and the law would be better enforced, if these offences were tried before ordinary justices of the peace, who are quite plentiful in Nova Scotia.
Under what authority does the minister take the right to appoint justices of the peace?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
It has been done ever since Confederation, I have not given consideration to the matter. I presume that former governments must have been satisfied as to their jurisdiction. I do not know that the 
right has ever been questioned in the courts in connection with this Act.

The moment you appoint a justice of the peace, you are creating a court, which, although it may be an inferior court, is a court nevertheless, and is within provincial jurisdiction, and not within the jurisdiction of this Parliament. The only federal court we ever created was the Supreme Court of Canada, and the authority for the creation of that court is expressly given in the British North America Act. It never seems to have been contended, that we could appoint a justice of the peace, except in connection with this Act, and perhaps the notion is borrowed from the Northwest Mounted Police Act, under which we have special authority from the Imperial Parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The Fisheries Act was
passed originally shortly after Confederation, and the Mounted Police Act did not come into existence until some years later. The notion, therefore, could not have been taken from the Mounted Police Act.

I am not sure that
this provision was in the original Fisheries Act. Whether it was or not, the mere fact that a thing should go unchallenged for forty-five years does not make it law. I do not like to ask any special favours for Nova Scotia, but I would urge that this law should not apply to that province because there is, I believe, a vicious principle in the law. A man certainly cannot lay information before himself.
Why not?

It would be so absurd that no reasonable man would do it, although apparently he could under this provision. There is a provision in the law that a justice of the peace must be satisfied thaf a cause of action exists before he can take an information. Of course, he could argue with himself and convince himself that there was a cause for action. I presume that he would not find very much difficulty, when he saw a man poaching on a river, in convincing himself that there was a reason for laying an information. He could criticise the information and see, to his own satisfaction, that it complied with the law. He would no doubt satisfy himself that the form of the information was satisfactory-that it complied with the law and that an offence was disclosed by it. As the information would be his own handiwork, he could easily satisfy himself upon that point. Of

course, he could swear himself; he could give evidence himself; he could crossexamine himself; he could at the same time take down the evidence, and he could believe or disbelieve himself just as he thought proper. It is possible that he would not believe himself. If so, then of course the accused would get away. There
is,	I think, a natural tendency for a man to believe himself, particularly when he is sworn by himself. This is a most extraordinary kind of court. It is well worth while for my hon. friend the minister to consider the matter. If this section were being put forward by somebody who was not a lawyer, I would be a little slower in condemning it; but as it comes from an eminent lawyer of vast experience, an exattorney general, and as it has passed through the hands of another distinguished lawyer as chairman of the committee, I think it gives another lawyer of some small experience like myself some justification for making a dead set upon it and killing
it,	if possible. If the minister will not say that he will let this section stand for the present, I shall be obliged to move that it be struck out. I make that motion subject to its being taken back, if the hon. minister will say that he will take this section into his consideration.

It is not very often
necessary to supplement anything that my hon. friend from Victoria and North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) says, because he usually covers the whole ground; but on reading over section 5 hurriedly, I feel that my hon. friend has not done justice to the powers of this fishery officer. It is quite true that the information will be laid before him, and I presume that he could issue the summons or warrant himself. He could try the case and believe or disbelieve himself; but, as I understand it, suhsection 3 of this section is something new, and has been added by the present minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
At present there is a section in the Act exactly similar to this one, except that it says:
The Governor in Council may appoint-
This gives the minister, without going to Council, the power of appointing these fishery guardians. The reason of the change is that for years, until two or three years ago, in spite of the provision in the Act that these fishery guardians had to be appointed by Orders in Council, they were 114}
never so appointed. Suddenly some one in the department awoke to the fact that these officers had to be appointed by Orders in Council; and, as it is merely a perfunctory matter on the part of the Council to appoint a man whom the minister recommends, it has been thought better to leave it in tne hands of the minister rather than in the hands of 'Council.
That only carries the matter to the point of absurdity, because we know that the minister would appoint as police officer the same man who was fishery guardian.
They are temporary employees.

Unless my hon. friend wants to provide places for his friends to a greater extent than we are charging him with doing, he will appoint the same man. Then this justice of the peace, witness and jury, could also be the officer who executes the warrant.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The hon. gentleman misunderstands the matter. The only persons whom the minister can appoint under this section are the fishery guardians. They are temporary employees; they are not fishery officers. They are obliged to do certain work during certain months of the year. The persons who would be vested with the powers of justices of the peace must be appointed by the Governor in Council.
What officers would they be?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Fishery inspectors and
fishery overseers. The fact of their being appointed fishery inspectors and fishery overseers by the Governor in Council does not at all vest them with the powers of justices of the peace. That has to be a separate matter. The hon. gentleman will see that the section reads:	[DOT]
The Governor in Council may appoint fishery officers whose powers and duties shall be as defined by this Act and the regulations made under it, and by instructions from the minister.
Then:
Every fishery officer, who is authorized by the Governor in Council to exercise the powers of a justice of the peace.
This has to be a separate authorization.
Subsection 3 refers to those people who are not classed as fishery officers, but are

simply fishery guardians. They are appointed by the minister.
That does not preclude my hon. friend from appointing the same persons with the dual capacity.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No, but it would be absurd to appoint the same man as fishery overseer and fishery guardian or as fishery inspector and fishery guardian.
If I understand my hon. friend from Richmond (Mr. Kyte) and other members from Nova Scotia aright, the department of my hon. friend is capable of doing a good many absurd things.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Nothing as absurd as that.
Take the case of Captain Landry and similar appointments.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The incident referred to by my hon. friend did not happen while I was minister; it happened while the other Government was in power.
Before 1896.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Well, that is a long time
ago-	->

In case I might forget it, I wish to say to the minister that when this Bill comes up for a third reading, I will move that subsection 2 of section 5 be struck out. I am not quite sure' what the procedure may be, but it would seem fair to tell the minister of my intention.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The procedure, I think, is very plain. On the motion for the third reading, the hon. gentleman will move that the Bill be not now read the third time, but that it be referred back to the Committee of the Whole, with instructions to amend the same in the manner he desires.
I do not know whether any notice is necessary or not.
I think it is not necessary in a public Bill, if it is required at all; it is only in a private Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: However, we can look up the practice.

I think my hon. friend (Mr. McKenzie) is only making sure that he is within the rule. Of course, it was a courtesy to the Government to_ inform them of his intention, but I think it is not necessary under the rule in the case of a public Bill. In the case of a private Bill notice must be given.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 12-fry, parr or smelt not to be killed:
Does this provide that a salmon weighing less than three pounds cannot be caught?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No; it can be caught with a hook and line.

Last year I had a call
from some friends who were going fishing, and who were told that they would not be allowed to catch salmon under three pounds. It is absolutely contrary to all the laws of human nature that a man, after catching a salmon weighing two and three-quarter pounds, should throw it back into the stream; it simply cannot be done.
