Could the minister give us the names of his chief officers in this department?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Brock is the deputy minister. Before being appointed deputy minister he was the director of the Geological Survey. He has not been replaced as director. Professor Haanel is director of the Mines Branch of the department; Mr. Marshall, accountant; Mr. Sauvalle, chief translator; Mr. Groves, editor. Other employees are:	Messrs. Marshall, Bell,
Paradis, Loux, Ainsborough, Levesque, Haanel, Wait, McLeish, Wilson, Frechette, McKenzie, Lindeman, Connor, Hudson, Stanfield, Blizard, Robinson, Ells, Casey, Cartwright, Cole, Von Anrep, Ogilvie, and Pereira.
The hon. gentleman, in . these various branches, has an increase of some twenty-five in the number of employees and of about $32,000 in salaries.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: There is an increase in the number of employees of fifteen, three in the department proper, six in the Mines Branch, and ten in the Geological Survey Branch. These new employees have been deemed necessary for the welfare of the department.
Are the new men appointed under section 21 of the Civil Service Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
The positions have not
been filled yet. We aTe creating the positions and fixing the salaries, and if the Estimates go through the appointments will be made later on, according to the law. Practically none of the appointments are made under section 21 of the Civil Service Act; they are nearly all made after competitive examination, according to the law.

The reason I asked that question in reference to the new appointments being made under the Civil Service Act, is that I find in several departments under the present Government things are found possible that were never found possible in my department when I was a minister. There were appointments that I desired to make as Minister of Railways and Canals, even of a minor character, but I was never able to get the Civil Service Commission to view the matter as I did, and I could not make those appointments. But under the present Government, in nearly all of the departments, appointments are made in a way that I was not permitted to make them. I was wondering if the Civil Service Commission had recanted, or if the Government had driven a coach and four through the Civil Service Commission and the law.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Probably my hon. friend is under a mistaken impression, because of

an answer which was given to a question put by the hon. member for Russell (M.r. Murphy) on the 11th February last, and which was not complete. The answer had been prepared by the Civil Service Commissioners, but after Hs production I found it was not complete. As the answer is found to-day on page 698 of 'Hansard,' it is only an enumeration which shows what appointments in all the departments have been made without any examination or competition. As a matter of fact, all these appointments have been made according to the law. The number of appointments given on that page is 361, and if this answer is followed up, it would seem that all of the 361 employees had been appointed by ministers in accordance with the provisions of the Civil Service Act. As a matter of fact, 101 of these employees have been nominated under section 21 without competitive selection; 48 have been nominated under section 21 after competitive selection by the commissioners, and 85 have been selected and appointed by the commission after special, open competition, that is to say, competitions which were held between May and November; 131 have been appointed under section 22 of the Act in the lower grades. For these appointments section 22 does not impose a competitive examination.
Mr. GRAHAM; That is the loop hole.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
This is for sorters,
messengers, and other officials lower than the third class. My hon. friend will see now that appointments by the Civil Service Commissioners according to section 21 are not as numerous as they would seem to be by a reading of the answer.
Mines and Geological Survey-Mines Branch -investigation of ore deposits economic minerals, peat bogs, determination of fuel values of coals, lignite and peat of Canada, including wages of machinist and labourers, and additional machinery; investigation of ore dressing, including housing of roaster, wages of labourers, machinery and equipment of laboratory; collection of information regarding minerals and metallurgical industries and operations, $86,000.

The question of ore deposits is a very large and important one.
I noticed in the report of the province of Ontario for this year that the value and quantity of output have very largely increased. If I remember correctly, the value is something like $52,000,000, which is certainly very encouraging. My own opinion is that we have in various parts of Canada mineral deposits of which we know very little at the present time. We have very large deposits of iron ore in the province of

Ontario which seem to be of a low grade. I was told the other day by one of our manufacturers of steel rails that they import at least ninety per cent of the ores to mix with ours. On the other hand, we export quite a quantity of low grade iron ore for use on the other side of the line. As far as export and import are concerned, they merely constitute an exchange. It would be of great value to the country if we could adopt some process that would enable us to utilize these low grade ores. It has been stated on several occasions that we have in Ontario what we call Bessemer ore and that in a short time we would be able to use a much greater percentage of our own ore in the manufacture of steel rails. Up to the present time the idea has not been brought to fruition. Could my hon. friend give the committee any information as to the prospects of our being able to use our own ore in larger quantities in the manufacture of steel rails?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I do not think I can
answer this question now, because, as my hon. friend said a few minutes ago, it is a fact that our iron ore is of such low grade *that those who are interested in the deposits have lately approached the Government in order to get a bonus. This question has not been decided yet. They claim that the grade of the iron ore being low, it is absolutely necessary to enable them to compete effectively with the American ores which are richer, to obtain assistance from the Government in one form or another. I have read in the papers that they have mentioned a bonus as being tiie form in which this assistance could be most advantageously given. But nothing has yet been decided in that matter.

I would like to ask the minister whether his department have made any investigations into the electrical process of smelting refractory ores in Canada.
I understand that the trouble with our ores is that they are either refractory or contain large quantities of sulphur.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I am told that the Government have had experiments made with the electrical process of smelting and that the results of these experiments have been supplied to the interested parties throughout Canada.

That would be by Dr.
Haanel.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
By Dr. Haanel. I may be allowed to add that about 17 per cent of

the iron ores smelted in Canadian furnaces during 1909 was of domestic origin. This small proportion is due to the fact that we have not as yet discovered merchantable deposits of sufficient magnitude to meet requirements. The iron and steel companies of the Maritime provinces, it is true, secure the major portion of their ore supply from Newfoundland; but the Ontario furnace-man is almost entirely dependent for his ore upon the American ranges of Minnesota and Michigan, and in 1909 he found it necessary to import from the United States over 71 per cent of the amount required. While our supply of merchantable ore in Canada is limited, we possess enormous quantities of low grade material, not so regarded, which have been, so to speak, in reserve and which have hardly been touched.
To render these impure ores in fit condition for the manufacture of iron and steel necessitates the application of a concentration process, and the fact that the vast majority of our low grade iron ores are of the magnetic variety suggests the adoption of magnetic concentration as a means whereby they may be utilized with profit. We are experimenting in the laboratory 'at Ottawa with the concentration process.
As a matter of fact; you have not made any progress in finding out a process which will make the smelting of our low grade ores commercially profitable?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: No, not yet.

That is one of the questions that comes up with the Government in discussing the suggested aid to this industry. Quite a number of those who ask for aid to the industry say that it ought to be confined, if any be given, to ores smelted in Canada. Others say that it should be given to ores smelted, or exported, or shipped. It would be oi great interest to the province of Ontario particularly, if it could be possible to discover a process by which our immense deposits of low grade ore could be made merchantable and profitable. Personally, T travelled considerably in the territory where these ores are found even before we knew we had silver deposits. I tramped over a good many of the ore prospects and it was then hoped that some process had about been discovered by which the value of this ore could be greatly increased. I want to find out if we have succeeded in finding that process or if we are still searching it.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Dr. Haanel, in a report upon this subject says:
The present installation will treat only a certain class of iron ores and by one method only. Additional machinery is required, if we are to undertake the testing of iron and other ores on a broad scale.
There is no testing laboratory in Canada sufficiently equipped to carry on experimental work of this character, and investigators are forced to go to the United States or elsewhere if they wish to make experiments of a practical nature When the Zinc Commission was investigating methods of metallurgical treatment for the lead-zinc ores of British Columbia they were obliged to carry on their experiments at Denver, Colorado, because there was no Canadian laboratory available. Our universities, it is true, possess well equipped and experimental laboratories, but they are used solely for educational purposes, and the experts or professors in charge have not the time, nor do they advertise their willingness to undertake work of public nature.
As previously stated, the present concentration plant is Installed in a small room originally intended for a repair shop. This necessitated unavoidable crowding of the various apparatus to an extent that absolutely precludes the possibility of adding additional machinery.
It is apparent that if we are to enlarge the present installation in the direction of a National Testing Laboratory more room is required. This may be secured in a comparatively inexpensive manner by building an addition to the fuel testing station, so that it forms a continuation, one story high, at the back of the present structure.
The addition should be large enough to accommodate the new apparatus required without dangerous crowding of machinery and at the same time afford plenty of space for any additional installation as may bei required from time to time. It is advised that the proposed addition should have a floor space of 57 by 60 feet. That is to say, the addition should have the full width (57 feet) of the present structure, extending 60 feet hack, and may he constructed hy simply adding three walls and a roof to cover this floor space, together. with the necessary partitions.
I would, therefore, recommend that the Public Works Department place in their Supplementary Estimates an amount to cover the construction of this addition. Provision has been made in the main Estimates of the Mines branch for the- purchase of the necessary machinery.
A couple of weeks ago the Department of Public Works purchased a site on which is to be erected the roasting ore building, in which experiments will be made on a larger scale. The company is asking a bonus from the Canadian Government because it claims that it cannot now concentrate on a commercial basis.
Where is this building to be situated?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Near the site of the fuel-testing plant.

I am inclined to think

that more real aid can be given to the industry by working out this problem for it than by giving it a bounty to experiment with itself. What progress -has (been made in experimenting with the manufacture of peat? Some years ago I took quite a little interest in the manufacture of peat into a marketable commodity for fuel. Having come very close, however, to some people who have invested in plants for the manufacture of peat, I have now become a doubting Thomas regarding it. Experiments have been carried on for some years, but I have yet to learn that a method has been discovered by which the peat in our peat bogs can be converted into marketable briquettes. No real advance has been made. I have feen tests made of the briquettes; they burn nicely and give out a fine heat, -but they have been only a spasmodic success and have been manufactured in small quantities. Can the minister tell us if the -people of Canada may expect our great peat bogs to be utilized in a practical manner? We have a sufficient amount of peat in the Dominion of Canada to protect us from all the coal barons in the world, if the Government has solved the problem how to manufacture peat. If I remember aright, the great difficulty was in getting rid of the moisture in the raw material. Another difficulty was that the briquettes though they looked very inviting at first, and produced the desired result, disintegrated in a very short time leaving very little behind but a few shovelfuls of mother earth.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
When I was appointed at the head of this department, I received a memorandum from Dr. Haanel, Director of Mines Branch, on that very subject. The memorandum was made after the experiments in Alfred, Ont., -had been completed. As my hon. friend will remember, the Government bought a peat bog in the province of Ontario a few years ago. A plant was installed there and experiments were made according to the air-dried process. In that memorandum Dr. Haanel stated that the experiments showed that it was possible -by that process to produce those briquettes in *such a way that the enterprise would pay commercially. A gentleman of the name of Shuttleworth, from London, England, h-as for years taken a great interest in that industry. I am told that he has already spent $50,000 in experiments with the air-dried process and with another process by -means of pressure. Mr. Shuttleworth wanted to buy the bog at Alfred, and the 
-Government plant there, and to work the -peat with the air-dried process, according -to the discoveries made in the work done under the supervision of Dr. Haanel a few years before. The Government sold- the peat bog to Mr. Shuttleworth.
For how much ?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Six dollars an acre. I do -not know what sum was paid for the plant.

Wh-at is the total amount received by the Government?
-Mr. CODERRE: $2,284.25. There are two companies to-day manufacturing peat, one at Alfred, Ont., and one at Fa-rn'ham, Ont. They have tried to produce briquettes on a commercial basis, and sell them at a price which would enable the peat to compete with coal. The Government give a subsidy of $1,500 a year to the Canadian Peat Society to encourage this industry.
Have these men made a commercial success of the industry? Did not your experiments amount to nothing, after all?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Shuttleworth bought the Alfred peat bog only six months ago, so that I have no report to show whether he has made it a success or not.
The minister has an item here for investigation of ore deposits, economic minerals, peat bogs, etc. He has sold the peat bog. What does he propose to do in regard to peat with any of this vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: To investigate other bogs and report as to the quality and quantity of the peat.
A gentleman at London, Ont., has been experimenting with peat at his own expense for some years. Did the department ever look into his process for recovering peat on a commercial basis?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I have no information
on this point.

His name is Dr. Mac-
William. Would it not be a good idea for the Government if they are expending money in trying to recover peat on a commercial basis, to look into Dr. MacWilliam's process and see what advance he has made? In Russia they -are able to recover peat on a commercial basis and sell it against coal or wood in very large quantities; but the process is by hydraulic pressure. I have a sample of the Russian peat at home, and it is superior to anything I have seen made

in Canada, although I have seen peat from the various Canadian peat bogs, made by the department and by others who have been trying to manufacture it. Why should not the Government look into the Russian process? We have enormous peat bogs all through the country. If we could manufacture peat on a commercial basis, there is no reason why we should not supply our people with this class of fuel. It is a success if it is properly manufactured. Peat produced by the air-dried process pulverizes and is no good.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Personally, I have no information on that subject. But the reports on the experiments made at Alfred with the air-dried process oblige me to come to a different conclusion from that which the hon. gentleman has stated. According to the reports, it has been demonstrated that it is possible by this process to produce briquettes of peat which will compete commercially with coal and wood as a fuel.
How long will it remain exposed to the air without pulverization?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: It was only after the report was made that this gentleman from London bought the Alfred bog and plant which the Government owned. The report and explanation given to him by Dr. Haanel convinced him that he could produce peat there on a commercial scale and at a competitive price. He has been experimenting since he bought the property, but the results of those experiments I do not yet know.

I know that every year since I entered this House there has been a vote of money for Dr. Haanel to carry on experiments with peat. I have read his reports so far as they have been printed; but the mere fact that nobody has taken hold of the property, nobody has invested money in it, except this Mr. Shuttleworth, who is making the experiments at a very low cost, proves to me that the practical men in the peat business do not believe that Dr. Haanel has discovered a process that can be made commercially .successful. I do not wish to say anything against Dr. Haanel, but I believe that the money which has been spent has been wasted so far as he has gone, and I feel more confident in that opinion because nobody has taken hold of this process with a view to supplying peat fuel in competition with coal. It is time we quit spending money
for nothing. I have no objection to spending money for anything of value, but to spend money year in and year out, as Dr. Haanel has done, on a process that he could have tried out in a year, is a waste of money.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
These experiments at
Alfred ended a few years ago, and the Government is not spending more money there. As I stated a few moments ago, the plant has been sold to Mr. Shuttleworth.
Apparently some part of this vote is to be spent there.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: That money will not be spent on experiments of the same kind. Part of it is for investigation of the various peat bogs in the country, to learn their extent and the quality of the peat in them.

This item is so mixed
up with other things that it is hard to tell what is going to be paid.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
This item covers the
following expenses:

in the field during the season. . .. [DOT] [DOT] ?56,000 Plant and equipment and operating
expenses of one dressing plant.. .. IMUO Plant and equipment and operating expenses of fuel testing station....[DOT]

(4)	Gold and copper deposits of the Yukon,

Does the minister think there is anybody in his department more capable of devising means for profitably smelting copper in any form than some of the Canadian copper companies? I am sure there are many large corporations interested in copper in this country which are quite capable of looking after any experiments that are to be made in regard to copper smelting.

We had a letter from the hon. Minister of Mines to-day announcing the distribution of a monograph on the coal resources of the world. There are many persons in France, capitalists and other gentlemen, who would be interested in this publication, and I wish to ask the minister whether he intends to have it translated into French?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: The monograph on the coal resources of the world will be distributed this week. The volume contains reports in German, English and French The matter as to whether or not the French will be translated into English and the English into French has not been taken into consideration. If this were done, that part of the report which is printed in German would have to be translated too and the expense would be great. This monograph is not an ordinary report of the department; we have to pay for it, and the price is rather large.
I understand that the report is published in three languages.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

Before we get too far away from the subject of peat, which was 
under discussion, and on which the hon. member for North Oxford contributed some valuable information, I would like to say that the opinion of practical men who are interested in the subject is that the experiments conducted by Dr. Haanel have been a failure, that the money which has been placed at his disposal has been wasted, and that no beneficial results have accrued, either to the Government or to the people interested in this industry, from that expenditure. The minister has told us that the plant and the peat bog at Alfred have been disposed of for $2,284.25. Would my hon. friend tell the committee what amount of money was expended by the Government at Alfred for the bog and the plant?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: If I remember well, the peat bog was sold for the price that was paid for it by the Government, $6 an acre. So far as the plant is concerned, Mr. Shuttleworth has bought only a part of it, paying what Dr. Haanel thought was a fair price for it. The Government expended a certain amount of money for a siding put there by the Canadian Pacific railway, and that money has been repaid by Mr. Shuttleworth to the Government. These various sums made up the total which I gave a few moments ago, $2,284.25, which represents the cost of the bog, siding and conveyancing fees.

Do I understand the
minister to say that the amount the Government has received represents the cost of the bog, the cost of a new siding and conveyancing fees?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
What nas been the total amount expended there in connection with Dr. Haanel's experiments ?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
The amount which has been spent, which includes the amount spent before as well as since I took office, amounts, I think, to $25,508.98. I am surprised to hear that the experiments conducted by Dr. Haanel have produced no good results. I may not be a good judge of the matter, but I have read Dr. Haanel's report with great interest, and he seems to be sure that these experiments have demonstrated that by means of
9 p.m. the process which has been followed there, peat can be put on the market on a commercial basis. He has told me that that process is the one which has been followed in Norway and Sweden, and of course the experiments in

those countries have met with considerable success. He does not know of any reason why, under the same circumstances, similar success should not be attained here by means of the same process.

I would point out that the mere saying that he believes it will be a success does not make it a success. My hon. friend has supplied the committee with figures showing that the difference between what the Government has received for its peat bog and plant and what has been expended represents an outlay of over |23,000, for which the Government or the people of the country have received no return. A few years ago Dr. Haanel was equally confident that he was going to work wonders in electrical smelting at the Sault. So far as I am personally aware, all that ever came from those experiments were a few rather ornamental paper weights; beyond that, I do not think the country ever saw anything as a result of those experiments. That being the case, I would like some further information from my hon. friend with reference to this plant and the experiments at Alfred. There are large deposits in the county of Russell which I have the honour to represent, and the plant at Alfred is situated almost on its eastern border, so that my constituents have a very live, practical interest in these experiments. I understood my hon. friend to say that his own opinion did not quite coincide with that expressed by Dr. Haanel. If that is so, my hon. friend's opinion is, I think, in harmony with the opinion entertained by the practical public generally. My .hon. friend stated that the plant at Alfred and the peat bog there had been sold to the Shuttleworth Company, of Brantford. He also stated that the company had made experiments there last summer but he did not know the result. My information is that the result has been a failure and that the plant has again been sold. Has my hon. friend any information as to the present owners of the plant at Alfred?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: No, this is the first intimation I have had that the Shuttleworth Company had sold it.

It has been demonstrated before the committee this evening that the ' experiments of Dr. Haanel have been anything but an economic success, and I would like to know if it is the intention of the Government to test any other process than the process that is alleged to have been under investigation by Dr. Haanel.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
There is no provision
for that in the Estimates.
What is the fuel-testing plant in the western part of this city used for?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
This plant is to test
fuel. It is used to test peat in the gas producer and also to test the heating qualities of Canadian lignites and coal, The fuel-testing plant could not be used to manufacture the peat or briquettes which have been produced at Alfred.

Will my hon. friend
afford any other gentleman or company who may have a process for the manufacture of peat an opportunity of having a test made at the plant in this city?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I do not know whether that experiment could be made. I am told it is very doubtful.

If a person like the gentleman mentioned by the hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt), interested m having a test made in which the country would be interested, applied to my hon. friend, would he afford opportunity for testing such a process, as has been done in the past by Dr. Haanel?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: This plant in Ottawa is for testing the quality of fuel, not to manufacture.

Is it a fact that Dr.
Haanel has advised that no further Government money should be spent on peat plants?
Mr. CODERRE? Yes, Dr. Haanel has told me that he could not recommend that any more money be spent, because he contends, as I said before, that he has found in that air-dried process the very means of producing peat on a commercial basis.

My hon. friend from
North Oxford has afforded proof that this is not the case, and I have a letter here corroborating that. Would my hon. friend 1st the committee know how much of the amount covered by the vote we are now considering is to be utilized by Dr. Haanel for any experiments he may be carrying on?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
$16,700 and $13,300, a
total of $30,000 for the ensuing fiscal year.

My further information
is that about $100,000 had been expended by Dr. Haanel, or under his direction, in connection with these peat tests, and that the result has been a complete failure. I would suggest to the minister, who is of

course not under any responsibility for the expenditure or the result, inasmuch as the department has only recently come under his charge, that he stop further expenditure until he has satisfied himself personally by the report of or on the authority of practical men, that some beneficial results are likely to be obtained from the expenditure of these large amounts of public money. Like the hon. member for North Oxford, I am not acquainted with Dr. Haanel; I do not know what his qualifications are; but I do know that there is a very general complaint about his methods and lack of results among that portion of the public to whom one would naturally look for practical information on the subject. My hon. friend from North Oxford inquired a short time ago how the money was spent.
I have here one item in a return giving the number of citizens of the United States who have been employed by the departments of the Government. I see a gentleman mentioned as having been engaged under an agreement with Dr. Haanel, to whom $6,000 were paid, to make a repo-t on the petroleum and natural gas resources of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: What year?

The year is not given, but this Teport was brought down at the present session. The gentleman's name is Mr. P. G. Clapp. It looks as if Dr. Haanel is given a free hand to spend public money when and how he pleases. He has engaged a gentleman at a salary far in excess of what the higher paid officials in the service are receiving. This report to which I refer contains the names of a number of other citizens of the United States, who apparently have been similarly engaged for possibly similar work. I would like the minister to tell the committee under what circumstances this particular gentleman, who received $6,000, was engaged, and how agreements came to be made with several other persons whose names are mentioned in this return as having been engaged by the Department of Mines.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Clapp is a petroleum expert who was engaged a year ago last summer. Four thousand dollars have been spent for himself and his party, and he has received $2,000 for his report.

I would like to know from my hon. friend if he would entertain a proposal likely to result in producing
fMr. Murphy.]
peat fuel that could be manufactured economically, and could be disposed of at a low figure, in competition with other fuels, to the public on a commercial basis.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I do not know. I have heard and read of the experiments which have been carried on in the past, first by the pressure process, and later by the air-dried process. The pressure process has not given satisfaction. I thought, after having read Dr. Haanel's Teport on the experiment with the air-dried process, that at last we had found something which might be of advantage to the commercial .communities. But, according to the statement of my hon. friend, that is not the result. We in the department have confidence in Dr. Haanel. While he may not have succeeded in all the experiments that he has been called upon to make, he has a great reputation, and we thought that this process could be relied upon. I want to *say to my hon. friend that personally I do not know.

My hon. friend would not reject any proposal in the direction of making a new experiment merely because Dr. Haanel has advised against the expenditure of any further money in that direction-a direction in which he has himself failed?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: No. My hon. friend reminds me that about six months ago a gentleman by the name of Mr. Graham came to my office and represented to me that he had another process, that he had found the true recipe for producing peat as fuel on a commercial basis. I listened to him many times, -but he did not seem to agree with Dr. Haanel. Since Mr. ,Biock was appointed deputy minister, he has met Mr. Graham, and I have received lately a report from Mr. Brock. Mr. Brock does not think Mr. Graham's proposal a proper one for the department to entertain. We have refused for these reasons to comply with the request of Mr. Graham that the Government should spend about $3,000 to buy a plant to enable him to proceed with his experiments.
Has the Government disposed of the peat plant and land at Alfred?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Yes, the Government
sold to Shuttleworth.

I have every confidence in Mr. Brock's opinion on this or on any other matter within the purview of his

office. If the minister relies on Mr. Brock he will not at any time go far astray. I am pleased to learn that, merely because Dr. Haanel has advised against a further expenditure of moneys, in a direction in which he himself has been a failure, the minister will not turn down any new proposal. What purpose does the fuel-testing plant, on which we spent $40,000, serve now?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
It is used for testing
peat as a producer of fuel gas, and also for testing lignite and coal.

Mr. Edmond Ory, of Lille, France, vice-president of the Western Collieries, near Frank, Alberta, has written to me complaining of certain regulations enacted by the Government some years ago. The Western Colleries, and other collieries, purchased from the Government years ago certain mining lands, and they are' now subject to a royalty of about ten cents per ton on the product. Some years after this purchase, legislation was passed by which no more coal mines could be sold, but the coal lands were leased for a long term, ninety-nine years, I think, and the royalty, on the product of these lands was fixed at five cents per ton, instead of ten cents per ton which the other collieries had to pay. There is a discrimination in this, and those who have to pay the ten cents a ton naturally and justly protest. This is an important question., as these gentlemen have invested a large sum of money in the collieries, and employ a great number of hands. I think it is only fair that their request should be complied with. Mr. Ory writes to me, because I became acquainted with him in Europe. When the Franco-Canadian Treaty was being negotiated, Mr. Ory, who is a good friend to Canada, had great influence with some of the ministers in France, and helped us very materially to obtain that treaty. My own opinion is that the Government should pass regulations, bringing all the mines under a uniform system. Mr. Ory has prepared a draft petition which I shall later present to the Secretary of State, but I am informed that it should perhaps be addressed to the Minister of the Interior.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman
sends me the petition, I shall give it my serious consideration.

The petition is addressed by Mr. Ory to the Secretary of State. I have now the petition drafted by Mr. Ory, and I shall read it so that the minister may become cognizant of it:
To the Honourable Louis Coderre,
Minister of Mines,
Ottawa.
Dear Sir,-On two different occasions, in January, 1906, and in August, 1911, we presented to your predecessor, the Hon. Frank Oliver, a petition explaining to him the difficult position which most of the mining companies of the Crowsnest Pass were in and asking him to agree to reduce from 10 cents to 5 cents the royalty charged by the Canadian Government upon every ton of coal mined.
In support of our claim, we pointed out that on account of the 1908 Coal Mining Act, the various coal mining companies were treated in a very unequal way. In fact, the owners of coal lands bought prior to the 1901 Coal Mining Act are exonerated from any royalty and several of our bordering neighbours and most serious competitors are in this advantageous position. The owners, who, as we have done, have bought their lands under the regulations of the 1901 Coal Mining Act, that is to say during the period from 1901 to 1908, have to pay a royalty of 10 cents. From 1908, the coal mining lands have been leased instead of being sold and the leaseholders pay a 5 cent royalty.
Consequently it happens that, the considerable amounts spent to acquire the coal mining lands, sums bearing no interest, the owners of these coal lands bought under the regulations of the 1901 Coal Mining Act, are charged with an excessive tax of 10 cents per ton whilst their competitors, the leaseholders who have had neither, to spend these amounts of money in order to acquire the coal mining lands, nor to bear the trials and the charges which weighed heavily on the new companies, are in a privileged position and only pay 5 cents per ton.
This is an inequality of treatment which must be brought to light, upon which we particularly draw the kind notice of your Government and which we point out with the strictest confidence in your personal sense of justice.
An inquiry has shown that out of eighteen companies four only have been able to pay dividends during the last ten years. Futher-more, one of them has just been put in liquidation and we have, ourselves, been obliged to shut down our oldest mine at Lille (Alberta) where for the last few years we have had heavy losses and which has cost us $1,500,000.
Since fifteen years we have invested in our concern about $5,000,000 without receiving any dividend. Canada has largely benefited of our endeavour and of the wages we have paid which actually amount to more than $800,000 yearly; all the advantages and profits coming from our concern have been profitable to your country only.
Is it not fair that the Canadian Government should discontinue to weigh upon our company to such an extent as to discourage and ruin us, and that they should leave us, by reducing the royalty and putting us on the same footing as our competitors, the hope of realizing at last a small profit?
In leaving us in the hopeless position in which we now are, under regulations which give the Government alone all the profits of the concern, the money from the north of France would fatally be diverted from Canada, for which we however feel such a great sympathy.
These facts, showing that the companies of

our coal mining district are undergoing a crisis and are unable to bear a tax which, as the royalty exceeds in most cases the net profit realized, call for a reform.
We beg to hand you herewith copies of the petitions presented to your predecessor in January, 1906, and August, 1911. The situation explained in these documents has become worse and it is very urgent that relief be given even in the interest of the other important trades supplied by our mines such as:	railways, smelters, cement works, etc.
The Canadian Government alone can improve this so alarming situation by reducing, as we are asking you, the royalty charged on the coal mined by the companies which are under the regulations of the 1901 Coal Mining Act, from 10 cents to 5 cents per ton.
Confident in your good-will and in your great sense of justice, we are, Dear sir Tours respectfully,
West Canadian Collieries, Limited,
(Sgd) A. Wicart,
Chairman.
(Sgd) Ed. Ory, Vice-Chairman.
February 21, 1914.
This letter was transmitted to me by Mr. Ory with the request that I put it into the hands of my hon. friend after I had looked it over. As I explained a moment ago, Mr. Ory is a personal friend of mine, and that is the reason why he comes to me. I believe under the circumstances that my hon. friend ought to take this request into his consideration and bring the matter before Council and obtain a decision in regard to it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The introduction of such a Bill has been under consideration by the Government. In fact, I think it was under the consideration of the late Administration, as Mr. Templeman had prepared a Bill which he was about to introduce. After the Bill was submitted for the consideration of the Government by the Department of Mines, some question arose as to how far it might 
conflict, in the terms in which it was framed, with provincial legislation. It was not desired, of course, to override provincial legislation even if we had the power to do so, except in so far as might seem to be absolutely necessary in the public interest. Some negotiation and discussion with provincial authorities have gone on, I believe, and I understand that the Bill has been submitted to the consideration of the parliamentary counsel. While I have not any personal knowledge of what has been done in that regard during the past few weeks, I am given to understand that the difficulties which have arisen are now almost altogether, if not altogether removed. If that be the case, the Bill will again come under the consideration of the Government. Probably at an early date my hon. friend the Secretary of State will be able to make an announcement.

My hon. friend the
Secretary of State says that they have not found a successful process of manufacturing peat by hydraulic pressure. A good friend of mine, who has been in Russia investigating the subject, and who is a very capable man in that line, tells me that a very successful process by hydraulic pressure .is employed by the Russian Government. So far as my experience has gone, and I have investigated this peat problem to a considerable extent, I find that the air-dried process has not been a success, owing to the fact that the peat pulverizes too quickly when it is exposed to the air.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: The Government do not intend to spend money on the air-dried process. So far as the other process mentioned by my hon. friend is concerned, the Government have not yet taken it into consideration. I may say to my hon. friend from Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) that I thought at first that the communication which he read to the committee should have been sent to me as Minister of Mines; but, after reflection, I believe that the royalty is imposed by virtue of a regulation passed by the Minister of the Interior, and I would suggest that the communication be sent to him. Of course, I myself will take the matter into consideration, because I am informed by Mr. Brock that he believes that something should be done in that matter along the lines referred to by my hon. friend.

I desire to ask the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), as a matter of information, is that particular section within the borders of Alberta?
'Mr. OLIVER: Yes.

I was struck with the same thing that the hon. member has brought to the attention of the House, some months ago, when I had occasion to prepare a short essay upon the natural resources of northern Canada. In addition to the tar sand of which he has spoken, there is an immense quantity of natural oil in that section of the country. It was so stated by prominent engineers, among them Mr. J. B. Tyrrell, who spent many years in that northern country. The indications are that there are the most wonderful oil possibilities there of -any part of the world. Without going into any extended remarks, I think that the suggestion of the hon. member for Edmonton is very timely. Only a short time ago I r-an across an engineer, who is a chemist as well, who had spent three months in that very section of country at an expense to himself of $1,500 to $2,000, and his report upon that section of country was very glowing, so much so that private capital will no doubt be interested in that part of northern Alberta along the Athabaska river at no distant day. I would join the hon. member for Edmonton in pressing upon the Government to make a speedy examination of that part of the country with a view to preserving this valuable natural asset for the people of Canada. Of course, it may be that this should come under the local Government of Alberta, but I should think that it is a work that might be fittingly done by the Dominion under this vote. Quite detailed statements of the resources of that country were given before a committee of the Senate in 1907, I think, many engineers testifying to the natural resources in minerals, both metallic and non-metallic, of that portion of northern Canada.

I am glad to join in the remarks of my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) and to support the -suggestion that the Government without undue delay undertake the investigation of these tar sands. I have been interested in this subject ever since I first talked with men who went to the Klondike by the Edmonton route. The tales they brought into the Yukon regarding the vast deposits of these tar sands interested me then, and since then I have read all the reports and other material I could secure on the subject. All reports of travellers who have gone over that territory agree that the area covered by these bituminous sands is very considerable. The depth of the deposit also is great. As to the quality, while it varies from point to point, 1 believe it averages fairly high as compared with bituminous sands in other parts of the world, for instance Trinidad and some of the Balkan States. Up to the present time it has been difficult to secure any capital to develop these sands because of lack of transportation. But now a railway is pushing north and shortly will bisect this bituminous sand area for many miles. I have

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: A few months ago one of the officials of the department, Mr. Ells, visited the Athabaska district for the purpose of examining tar sand conditions there and making a report. He obtained several samples, which are being examined here and in New York. As soon as the investigations which are being carried on are completed, the report will be printed and distributed. The same may be said of the question raised by the hon. member for Kings, N.S. Officials of the department have been on the ground, have made examinations and taken notes, and the report will be prepared and distributed in due course. Certainly a reform is necessary so far as the printing and distributing of the reports of the Mines Branch are concerned. I am glad that the hon. member for Yukon has brought the matter up. A few weeks ago, speaking with my deputy in regard to the matter, we 10 p.m. came to the conclusion that these reports should be printed and distributed more promptly, and, on account of the lack of space in the Printing Bureau, we see no other means of doing so than by having them printed outside. A certain firm in Ottawa has been consulted; I do not know what action will be taken, but something will be done along that line as soon as possible,
Has the report of the investigation made by the officer mentioned by my hon. friend been printed yet?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: No; as soon as the result of the investigations are made known, the report will be printed. I cannot tell exactly when it will be available.
When was the investigation made ?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Last summer.

I wish to commend the department very strongly for having made an examination of the tar sand, and for having undertaken a thorough investigation of the quality and properties of the material secured. Although an undue length of time has elapsed since the investigation was made by the officer of the department, the public have not yet got the results of that investigation. This is an instance closely in line with the conditions alluded to by the hon. member for Yukon. Matters move fairly fast in this country, particularly in the West, and it seems to me that, the expectation being that there will be material results, the value of the investigation is seriously minimized by delay. This examination was made, my hon. friend says, last summer. If the results of that investigation were available to the public to-day, any capital which might become interested because of the investigation and its results would have the whole of the coming summer in which to operate, but if the result of the investigation does not become available to the public until some time during the coming summer, then action by capital cannot be secured until the following season, that is, two years from the date on which the examination was made. I .am quite aware that scientific people do not consider the material or economic sides of the matters with which they are concerned, but it is the business of the Government to see that the material and economic sides are considered. I submit that in this particular case the fact that there will be an -unnecessary delay of a full year before action can be had on the examination that was made, leaves the Government and the department open to serious criticism, for not having given the public the full advantage of the expenditure that has been made. I wish to commend the department for the measure of actual experiment that they have undertaken; but I wish to repeat and emphasize the importance of the practical work which should be undertaken in this connection. The examination and analysis of the tar sands that have been brought out is, of course, entirely desirable. But I am asking the Government to concentrate their attention upon the necessity of road making in that country and the possibilities of those tar sands for road making. While a chemical analysis will no doubt afford information to a certain degree, more than analysis is required, there must be actual experiment on a commercial scale before really 115
valuable information can be secured and it is for that purpose that I trespass upon what I may call the inattention of the minister a second time. It may be that this material will have no value for road making, -and that possibility precludes action by private capital and enterprise in demonstrating its use. It is for that reason that we ask the Government to make the experiment out of this vote. On the other hand, I believe that the probabilities are good enough to warrant the Government in making that expenditure.
i Mr. CODERRE: I am informed that the official who went to that district to study these tar sand deposits returned to Ottawa only in the latter part of October and has since been studying the material he brought with him. It will be understood that the -more care there is exercised in the studies and investigations the more valuable the results to the general public will be. I understand that the report will soon be ready and it will then be published and distributed. Does my hon. friend mean by actual experiment- that the Government should go into road making?
Experimentally.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: If the results of the tests that are going on in New York and Ottawa demonstrate that these tar sands are useful for road making, while I do not know if the Government could go into the actual experiments, still if we can and have the money available for the purpose, we will try to do something on -that line.

The minister has absolutely caught.the idea I wished to convey. I quite appreciate that it is desirable to understand the properties of these tar sands before it would be advisable to undertake actual experiment; it is in order to induce this Government to make actual -experiments that I have so strongly urged my case to-night. In order to serve an absolutely useful purpose, the Government would have to take a further step and carry on actual experiments to a sufficient degree and on a sufficiently large scale to demonstrate the possibilities of these tar sands in road making. Possibly these tar sands may contain a number of elements that may have many different uses.
I am not urging that the Government should take steps in regard to any of its other possible uses; I am urging the idea of the possibilities in regard to road improvements. If the analysis that is now being made demonstrates to the satisfaction of



the Government that the material is of no value, they would not be warranted in going farther, but if the test now being made indicates that this material has a road-making value then my urging is that they go on and make an actual experiment so as to demonstrate the fact. A railway is being built into that country and if actual demonstration has proven the value of this material for road-making, once the railway is completed, the work of the development of the tar sands and of road improvements in the prairie country can go on together. Unless there is a demonstration in the interval, before the road is completed, there will have to be a measure of time lost after the road is completed before the article can be used where it is so much required.
Mines Branch-Investigation of metallurgical problems of economic importance, $10,000.

I would like to draw the attention of the hon. Minister of Mines (Mr. Coderre) to the very great importance of having his officers keep a lookout for any radium ore. Radium is an element that is becoming of increasing importance particularly in the medical world. Some of the things that have been done with it border seemingly on the marvellous. Although I do not know of any ores in Canada which contain radium, it is possible that there are some. I was glad to notice the other day that the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Borden), in replying to a question which was directed at the Government, gave us the assurance that the Government was paying some attention to this very important element.
The Ontario Government have offered $25,000 for the discovery of radium.

Yes, the Ontario Government have offered a bonus of $25,000 to any man who will discover, within the fou * corners of the province of Ontario, radiumbearing ores. The United States Government have retired from entry all lands containing radium-bearing ores. In Austria, where the present supply, I understand, comes from chiefly, they have passed an * Act prohibiting the export of any of their radium-bearing ores. It seems to me, in view of the very great importance and of the potentialities of this mysterious element, that it might be worth the consideration of our Government, not only to retire from entry for the present these ores, but to offer to the world a substantial bonus for

the discovery of radium-bearing ores. If that were done the prospectors throughout the length and breadth of our country would apply themselves to the discovery and th'e reduction of some of the minerals which contain radium, such as pitchblende, car-notite, and autunite. I find, upon looking into this interesting subject, that in the whole world there is only about one and one-third ounces of radium. That has come chiefly from Austria. The European exploiters of this very expensive mineral have somewhat raised the price. It is an exceedingly difficult thing to secure. In the first place, it seems to be exceedingly rare, and judging from the history of radium up to the present time, it is very expensive to reduce the ores and recover the radium salts. The Government of the United States are paying some attention to this matter. The Government of Ontario have already offered a bonus and I understand that the Government of British Columbia are also following along the same lines. I submit for the consideration, and I hope the favourable consideration, of my hon. friend the Minister of Mines that he might take this matter up with the Government and, if at all possible, offer to the prospectors and people in Canada who are interested in our minerals a substantial bonus for the discovery of radium-bearing ores.

The other day I had a question on the Order Paper in reference to this matter, and it was answered by the Government. I wish to emphasize what the hon. gentleman (Mr. A. Thompson) has said. The reason I put that question on the Order Paper was this: I had had a good deal of correspondence with a gentleman who persists in believing that he knows where there is a deposit of these ores. He feels very confident on the subject. If that be the case, I think this country ought to do anything in reason to encourage the exploration and discovery, if possible, of these ores. Of course, this man, like many other prospectors, may be wrong, but he thinks he is right, and he is not in a position to go out and secure these ores unless some aid is given to him.

I would suggest to the
minister that he reserve the radium in these ores.
An Order in Council was passed the other day having that object in view.

That will be a powerful
order.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
As far as this question is concerned, I can only >say to my hon. friend from the Yukon (Mr. Thompson) that a pamphlet is being prepared by the Department of Mines which will give the necessary information to prospectors. Field parties will look for radium-bearing minerals during the coming summer. I remember that quite recently my hon. friend the member for Yukon spoke to me about the question of a bonus. The deputy minister has prepared a memorandum on that point which will be brought before the Government very soon. I do not know what the Government will do, but I feel assured that serious consideration will be given to the subject.
Mines Branch-For apparatus and equipment, salaries of inspectors, chemist, machinist, clerical assistance, and travelling expenses in connection with the investigations of the manufacture and storage of explosives in Canada, $55,000.
Will the minister tell us what the department does in reference to the investigation of explosives?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
A Bill concerning the
manufacture, storage and transportation of explosives will be presented to Council soon, and, if approved, will be submitted to the House. If it becomes law a certain amount of this money will be immediately applied.
Geological Survey Branch-Explorations and surveys, $175,000.
I wish to know why Mr. M. H. McLeod was dismissed from the Geological Survey.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I am told his engagement terminated two years ago.
Why ?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
The deputy minister
tells me that Mr. McLeod was never a permanent employee, and was only employed in field parties during the summer months.

Mr. McLeod had been in this service for the last thirty years, and he was admittedly very efficient in his particular work. He devoted his whole life to the collection and classification of rock, and there are letters extant from Mr. Fletcher and Mr. Selwyn who speak of him in the highest terms. True, he was only employed for nine months in the year at field work, but in winter he was usually employed by the department doing clerical work. Mr. McLeod did not take any part in politics. As a matter of 1154
fact, he has taken no part in politics of late years, and he was not at home last election. It is extraordinary that such a man, with such high attainments and such a high reputation in the service, should be summarily notified that his services were no longer required. In justice to Mr. McLeod, he should be told why his services were dispensed with, and I must insist on getting that informa tion. If all the rock in Canada has already been classified, I can understand, but perhaps it is that some day in the past he is supposed to have voted Liberal, and his sin is visited upon him by the Government.

Perhaps he had a relative who did.
,Mr. CHISHOLM: That may be, but I will not discuss that until I get the information.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: A return was prepared, which I laid on the table of the House some few days ago, and on perusing that return carefully I did not see stated in it why Mr. McLeod was dismissed. Personally I have no knowledge of the case, but if the hon. gentleman wishes me to ask the minister who was in the department at the time, I shall do so.

I realize that the present minister could not be personally aware of the facts, but I have a strong suspicion that Mr. McLeod has been dismissed for no other reason, than on account of representations made by personal enemies of his in the county. That being so, I expect the present minister to do Mr. McLeod the justice of offering him his position back again. You can realize what a desperate case this is; here is a man who has spent thirty years of his life to become efficient in a particular line of study, and when his services become most valuable to the country, he is driven out of office. Mr. Fletcher wrote several years before, that a better man could not be got for this work, and Mr. McLeod's services having then been dispensed with Mr. Fletcher succeeded in getting him reappointed to office. It is a deplorable thing that a man like Mr. McLeod should be put out of the service on the representations of some irresponsible parties. I know that he is not a political partisan; if he were I would not stand up here to defend him. In justice to the department, in justice to the Government, in justice to the public service, the minister should offer Mr. McLeod his position back again. I do not know

that Mt. McLeod will accept the position, in view of the shabby treatment he received. If I were in his place I would not, unless sheer necessity drove me to it, but anyhow it would be a decent thing for the minister to take such action. I ask that one of these items be allowed to stand until the information is brought down, as to why Mr. McLeod was dismissed.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Will any item do?
If the minister assures me that I can bring the matter up again, if the information is not given, I shall be satisfied.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Certainly.

How many parties will
be employed in northern Alberta during the coming season and what lines will be followed?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: We will have in northern Alberta two geological parties, and one topographical party for mapping.
What will be their field of observations? What locality will they traverse?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Lake Athabaska will be the operating base. One of the parties will work north of the lake and the other south o t it.
East or west of the Athabaska river?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: East of the river.
Both on the north and the south side of the lake?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
Where will the third party work?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: The third party will be the topographical party, to complete the work of the survey of lake Athabaska and its tributaries.
Are the purposes of these parties, which will operate north and south of the lake, scientific or economic?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Both scientific and economic?

I hope that, when the
parties return in the fall, we shall be able to get the results of their efforts before the close of the following winter.

Geological Survey Branch-For collection and purchase of specimens for Victoria Memorial Museum, $15,000.

Mr. Chairman, before that item is passed, I would like to make a suggestion to the hon. minister in connection with the Victoria museum and the Archives Department. As these buildings are visited every day by a large number of people, it is important there should be there men able to speak both languages.
1	visited recently the Archives Department. It contains many things of great interest, but we would take a much keener interest in them if we had the help of guides speaking the French language. Of course the men there are most obliging and courteous and extend all the information they can in their own language; but we are not in a position to gather their whole meaning, as if the explanations were given to us in French. I may add that we are often accompanied, we members from the province of Quebec, by persons who do not understand a single word of English. So we are bound to act as interpreters for the benefit of the people accompanying us, and it goes without saying that we are not always in a position to give as good satisfaction as if the explanations were tendered direct by men in a position to describe in the French language the works of art, paintings and other objects exhibited in the various departments.
I think that if the hon. minister would accept the suggestion I have just made, he would be doing something which would be appreciated throughout a great part of the province of Quebec, as well as by Frenchmen who visit this country. Surely old country Frenchmen who pass through Ottawa do not fail to pay a visit to the Victoria museum and the Archives.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
The Victoria museum is open to the public every week day from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., and on Sundays from
2	to 5 p.m. The men who attend on visitors belong, to the Dominion police staff. My department has no control over those men. I am at a loss to say to what department my hon. friend should apply, but it is certainly not to the Department of Mines. I am informed those men are under orders from the Department of Public Works.
Progress reported.
On motion of Mr. Rogers, the House adjourned at 10.42 p.m.
Thursday, March 19, 1914.
